6. Map background & search

Google and Bing have no free keyless tile URL. Paste the tile URL from your own API account into Custom. Placeholders: {z} {x} {y}, {q} = Bing quadkey, {s} = subdomain a–c.

7. Coastline & land avoidance
No coastline loaded. Close an area first.

OSM coastline is worldwide, full detail, user-contributed, so check it against official charts. For offline work, export GSHHG (full), Natural Earth 10m or OSM land polygons to GeoJSON and load the file. Turn paths are not checked against land.

8. Coordinate system for imported files
No EPSG CRS loaded.

Lookups use epsg.io or spatialreference.org and are cached in this browser, so codes you have used work offline later. The full EPSG dataset is not embedded. Datum grid files (NTv2 etc.) are not supported.

Values in the grey boxes come from the selected system; choose Custom to edit them. Shifts use a 3-parameter Molodensky transform (about a metre).

9. Survey boundary import
Supported: SHP (+PRJ, or a ZIP), DXF, KML, KMZ, GPX, GeoJSON, WKT, CSV/TXT vertex lists. Select the .shp and .prj together.

CRS: KML, KMZ, GPX and GeoJSON are WGS84 by specification. SHP uses its .prj file when present. DXF, WKT and text lists carry no CRS, so they use the coordinate system in section 8. DWG is a closed binary format and cannot be read in a browser: save it as DXF first (AutoCAD, BricsCAD, ODA File Converter or LibreDWG). If several shapes are found, the largest closed one becomes the boundary.

10. Global bathymetry (online, free)
Close an area first (draw, preset or import), then fetch.

The data are only as good as the source: GMRT and NCEI hold real multibeam surveys in places but are 100–450 m grids elsewhere, so use them for planning, not as a substitute for your own soundings. Land and drying cells are ignored. Vertical datum is roughly mean sea level, not chart datum: use the vertical offset in section 11 or choose a conservative depth. If your browser blocks a service (offline or CORS), use the link shown to download the grid and load it here. Sources: GMRT (Lamont-Doherty), NOAA NCEI, EMODnet, GEBCO via Open Topo Data (1 request per second, 1000 per day).

11. Bathymetry from XYZ file (your own data)

Horizontal coordinates use the system chosen in section 8. Soundings loaded here replace any global data.

Map sheet, PDF report and images

A hydrographic-style plan sheet with graticule, scale bar, north arrow, legend and title block. Printed at 100 % the scale bar is true.

GPX, KML, GML and NMEA are always WGS84 lat/lon. CSV, TXT, WKT, MIF and LNW follow the coordinate system chosen above. The HYPACK LNW layout is written from memory, so test-import it. DWG cannot be written from a browser: open the DXF in AutoCAD or BricsCAD and Save As DWG (or use ODA File Converter). The .LNX layout is written from memory of the HYPACK format; test-import before field use.

EIVA RLN follows the Helmsman runline format (E, N, KP). The Qinsy .qgfline file is rebuilt from a single sample file, so test-import it first. It uses WGS84 UTM (zone from the area centre) and straight lines only. Qinsy also reads DXF, DWG and KML.

Plan checks

    SwathPlan: guide and scientific background

    © 2026 Aldwin Syahperdana

    1. What SwathPlan does

    SwathPlan plans multibeam echosounder (MBES) survey lines. From a survey boundary, the water depth, the sensor swath angles and the overlap you want, it lays out parallel lines, designs the vessel turns, estimates time and distance, and checks the plan against the IHO S-44 order you choose. It runs entirely in your browser; only the map tiles and the global bathymetry downloads need internet.

    2. Quick start, step by step

    1. Define the survey area. Click Draw area and click the map to add vertices (double-click or Close polygon to finish), pick a port from Area presets, or import a boundary in section 9 (SHP, DXF, KML/KMZ, GPX, GeoJSON, WKT, CSV). Use Go to in section 6 to find any place.
    2. Set the coordinate system (section 8) before importing files that carry no CRS (DXF, WKT, text, XYZ). Choose geographic, UTM, a custom Transverse Mercator, or an EPSG code.
    3. Get the depth. Type a design depth (section 1), or load XYZ soundings (section 11), or fetch free global bathymetry (section 10). Then use Apply shallowest / 5th percentile / mean to set the design depth.
    4. Choose the sensor (section 1) and set the port and starboard swath angles (section 2). The catalogue values are approximate; check your datasheet.
    5. Set the overlap (section 2), typically 20–30 %. Tick Adaptive line spacing if you loaded depth data and want wider spacing in deeper water.
    6. Set the line direction (section 3). Auto optimal finds the azimuth with the fewest lines. Lines parallel to the contours usually give the most uniform depth along each line.
    7. Set the turn radius and speed (sections 4 and 5). Use Recommend R from LOA for a first guess, then enter your vessel's real turning radius.
    8. Pick the IHO order (section 5) and review the TVU, ping-rate and speed figures.
    9. Add the coastline (section 7) if the area touches land, so lines are trimmed with a safety clearance.
    10. Fill in the project and operations panel: start date, hours per day, weather allowance, SVP casts, calibration, mob/demob and the day rate if you want a cost estimate.
    11. Read the summary and Plan checks under the map. Fix any ⚠ items and iterate.
    12. Export (section 13) to your acquisition software (DXF, shapefile, KML, GPX, CSV, HYPACK, Qinsy QGF line, EIVA RLN, QGroundControl, Mission Planner and more), and create the printable report for the client.

    3. Panel reference

    • 1 Sensor & depth: model list (editable catalogue, CSV import) and design depth.
    • 2 Swath & overlap: angles, overlap, adaptive spacing, maximum spacing and swath width.
    • 3 Line direction: azimuth slider, presets, auto-optimal, cross lines and line names.
    • 4 Williamson turn: turn radius, vessel length, speed reduction in turns.
    • 5 IHO S-44 & speed: survey order, ping-rate limit, TVU, speeds.
    • 6 Map & search: basemaps (OSM, topo, satellite, ocean, custom tile URL), OpenSeaMap overlay, place search.
    • 7 Coastline: OSM coastline (online) or your land polygons, with clearance.
    • 8 Coordinate system: parameters shown for the chosen system; editable for Custom.
    • 9 Boundary import: reads CRS from .prj, or uses section 8 when the format has none.
    • 10 Global bathymetry: GMRT, NOAA NCEI, EMODnet, GEBCO, or a downloaded GeoTIFF/ASCII grid.
    • 11 XYZ: your own soundings with datum, unit and tide offset handling.
    • 12 Quick calculator and 13 Export.

    4. Scientific background

    4.1 Swath geometry

    A multibeam sonar forms a fan of beams across the track. For a flat seabed at depth d and beams steered to angles θp (port) and θs (starboard) from the vertical, the ground swath is

    W = d · ( tan θp + tan θs )          (m)

    Example: d = 25 m, ±60° gives W = 25 × 2 × 1.732 = 86.6 m, or 3.5 × depth. Because W grows linearly with depth, shallow water gives narrow swaths and many lines. In practice the usable angle is limited by signal-to-noise ratio, sound-speed refraction near the outer beams, sea state and the sensor's design, so the planner lets you cap the angle and the swath width.

    4.2 Overlap and line spacing

    Adjacent swaths overlap so that the noisy outer beams are backed up by good inner beams and no gaps appear. With overlap fraction o (overlap width divided by swath width) the spacing is

    S = W · ( 1 − o )                    e.g. 86.6 × 0.70 = 60.6 m

    The number of lines is N = ⌈B / S⌉, where B is the across-track extent of the area. In uniform mode the design depth should be the shallowest depth in the area (conservative); the 5th percentile is a common compromise.

    Adaptive (variable) spacing. The swath at each place depends on the local depth, so a fixed S wastes lines in deep water. SwathPlan places each new line as far from the previous one as the depth allows. For consecutive lines k and k+1 at across-track positions s and s′, with local depths dk(t) and dk+1(t) along the line coordinate t, the half-swaths facing each other are hk(t) and h′k+1(t), and the required condition is

    s′ − s  ≤  min over t of [ h(t) + h′(t) − o · ( W(t) + W′(t) ) / 2 ]

    The largest s′ that satisfies it is found by bisection. Because the vessel reverses direction on alternate lines, the starboard and port angles swap each line, and the code accounts for this. The first and last lines are placed so that the swath reaches the boundary. The method assumes flat seabed under each swath at the depth beneath the line, which is the usual planning approximation.

    4.3 Ping rate and along-track coverage

    A ping must travel to the farthest slant range R and back before the next ping, so the maximum ping rate is

    f max = c / (2 R),   R = d / cos θmax,   c ≈ 1500 m/s

    At d = 25 m and 60° the slant range is 50 m and fmax = 15 Hz. The along-track spacing between pings is Δx = v / f (v in m/s). The along-track footprint at nadir is about d · β, where β is the along-track beamwidth in radians. To detect a small object, several pings should land on it. The summary uses a rule of thumb of three pings on the smallest feature required by the chosen IHO order, which gives a maximum speed vmax = f · T / 3. This is a planning guide, not an S-44 requirement.

    4.4 IHO S-44 uncertainty model

    IHO S-44 limits the total vertical uncertainty (TVU) at the 95 % confidence level as

    TVU max(d) = √( a² + (b · d)² )
    Ordera (m)bTHU maxFeature detectionFull seafloor search
    Exclusive0.150.00751 mcube > 0.5 mRequired
    Special0.250.00752 mcube > 1 mRequired
    1a0.50.0135 m + 5 % of depthcube > 2 m (to 40 m depth), 10 % of depth deeperRequired
    1b0.50.0135 m + 5 % of depthnot specifiedNot required
    21.00.02320 m + 10 % of depthnot specifiedNot required

    Example: Exclusive order at 25 m gives TVU = √(0.15² + (0.0075 × 25)²) = 0.24 m. The values are those of S-44 as the author understands them; always check the current edition. Total uncertainty combines many independent error sources (sonar range and angle, sound speed, motion, tide, positioning), see Hare (1995).

    Cross-line check. Crossing lines are used to check consistency. If two independent measurements each have uncertainty TVU, their difference has uncertainty √2 · TVU, so differences at crossings should stay within about √2 · TVU(d) at 95 %. The summary shows this value.

    4.5 Williamson turn geometry

    To run the next line in the opposite direction, the vessel leaves the end of a line and turns around. If the line gap S is at least the turning diameter 2R, a plain U-turn with a straight connector of length S − 2R is used. If S < 2R, a Williamson-style turn is designed: turn away from the next line by an angle α, then turn the opposite way by 180° + α, ending on the reciprocal heading. The lateral displacement after the two arcs is

    S = 2 R cos α   →   α = arccos( S / 2R )
path length = R α + R (π + α) = R (π + 2α)
forward overshoot beyond the line end = 2 R sin α

    Example: R = 35 m, S = 60.6 m gives α = 30.0°, path length 146.6 m and overshoot 35 m. Real vessels and USVs have limited yaw rate and slow down in turns, so enter a realistic radius and the turn-speed reduction.

    4.6 Time and productivity

    on-line time  = (Σ line lengths) / v
turn time     = (Σ turn lengths) / v turn
productive    = on-line + turns
total project = (productive + SVP + calibration) / (1 − w) + mobilisation

    where w is the weather/downtime fraction. SVP time is the number of casts (productive time divided by the interval) times the cast duration. Duration in days divides the total by the operating hours per day. On-line efficiency is on-line time over productive time; a low value means turns dominate, so consider longer lines or a smaller overlap. Estimated soundings are pings × beams, with pings = ping rate × on-line time.

    4.7 Coordinates and datums

    The map works in a local metric frame around the area's centre (an equirectangular approximation, accurate for areas of some tens of kilometres). Geographic coordinates are converted to UTM or a custom Transverse Mercator with the series formulas of Snyder (1987), and the inverse series is used to read projected data. Datum shifts to WGS84 use the abridged Molodensky transformation with three translation parameters (typical accuracy a few metres, or better with local parameters). EPSG codes are resolved to PROJ definitions and converted with the proj4js library; datum grid files are not supported.

    4.8 Coastline and land avoidance

    OpenStreetMap coastlines are oriented with land on the left and water on the right. Each survey line is intersected with the coastline segments; the line is cut at the crossings, the starting side is decided from the nearest segment, and a clearance zone (a capsule of radius equal to the safety distance around each segment) is removed. For land polygons the inside/outside test is used instead. Turn paths are not checked against land.

    4.9 Bathymetry data sources

    SourceCoverageTypical resolutionNote
    GMRTGlobal≈ 100 m where multibeam exists, GEBCO elsewhereRyan et al. (2009)
    NOAA NCEI DEM mosaicGlobalCoastal DEMs to a few metres, ETOPO 2022 (15″) elsewhereMixed vertical datums
    EMODnet BathymetryEuropean seas≈ 115 m (1/16′)Digital terrain model
    GEBCO 2020Global≈ 450 m (15″)Via Open Topo Data

    These grids blend many surveys of very different quality and are referenced roughly to mean sea level. They are good enough to size a plan, but they cannot meet S-44 depth accuracy and may miss shoals, wrecks and channels. Use your own soundings or a reconnaissance line for final planning in critical areas.

    5. Assumptions and limitations

    • Flat seabed under each swath; no refraction or beam-angle limits other than those you enter.
    • Sound speed 1500 m/s for ping-rate limits.
    • Straight, parallel lines. Curved or contour-following lines are not generated.
    • Catalogue sensor data are approximate and may be out of date; "n/a" means unknown.
    • Time estimates assume constant speeds and ignore currents, traffic and port calls.
    • Coastline data are not a navigation chart. Always plan against official charts and local notices.
    • The Qinsy .qgfline file is rebuilt from a single sample and the HYPACK LNW layout is written from memory; test-import before field use.
